```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
```

## Background

[Horsfield et al.](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.02.04.703695) fitted a mechanistic
pangenome model (Pansim/PopPUNK-mod) to 408 bacterial species, estimating three
parameters per species: **basal gene turnover rate** (the minimum rate at which
accessory genes are gained/lost), **core mutation rate**, and the **proportion of
fast genes** (the fraction of the accessory genome exchanged essentially
instantaneously each generation). They found that inter-species differences in
pangenome size and structure are driven predominantly by variation in the
*proportion* of rapidly-exchanged genes, with the *rate* of exchange of the
remaining ("slow") genes conserved across species, and that this variation tracks
phylogeny rather than ecology.

[Kwun & Croucher](https://doi.org/10.1093/ismejo/wrag256) proposed and tested a
distinct mechanistic explanation for cross-taxon variation in genome plasticity:
an intragenomic conflict between homologous recombination (HR), which transformable
bacteria can use to delete chromosomally-integrated mobile genetic elements, and
prophage, which have evolved to detect and escape RecA-nucleoprotein filaments by
inducing lytic activation. Across 23 bacterial taxa, they found a significant
negative relationship between the probability of diversification through HR
(estimated from MLST data) and the expected number of intact prophage per genome
(estimated from complete genome assemblies).

This document tests the hypothesis that **the HR/prophage conflict identified by
Kwun & Croucher can explain the pangenome-scale variation reported by Horsfield et
al.** by merging the 23-taxon HR/prophage dataset with the corresponding
PopPUNK-mod parameter estimates, pangenome-size statistics, and (where available)
negative-exponential core-vs-accessory distance curve fits, from Horsfield et al.'s
Supplementary Files 1 and 8.

::: {.callout-note style="border-left: 4px solid #4C72B0; padding: 0.5em 1em; background: #f4f8fc;"}
**Scope of "prophage" in this analysis.** Throughout, prophage content refers
specifically to Kwun & Croucher's geNomad-based estimate of the expected number of
large, hallmark-gene-rich **Caudoviricetes** provirus regions per genome (`lambda_hat`)
— i.e. temperate phage plausibly capable of lytic induction and host-cell death, the
process through which HR and prophage are hypothesised to conflict. Satellite
phage/phage-related chromosomal islands (e.g. PRCIs), *Inoviridae*, and plasmids were
excluded from Kwun & Croucher's cross-taxon genomic comparison and are therefore
also excluded from every analysis below. Pangenome-size statistics will necessarily
also reflect the contribution of these other mobile genetic element classes, which
are not independently modelled here.
:::

```{r load-data}
datasets  <- build_analysis_datasets(raw_dir = "data/raw")
full_df   <- datasets$full_df     # all 23 taxa, merged with Supplementary File 1
negexp_df <- datasets$negexp_df   # 15 taxa with a Supplementary File 8 curve fit
```

### Taxa included

```{r taxa-table}
full_df %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(lambda_hat)) %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    Taxon                        = species,
    Transformability,
    Niche,
    `Isolates (n)`                = n_isolates,
    `Expected prophage / genome`  = round(lambda_hat, 2),
    `HR probability`              = round(`Recombination probability`, 2),
    `Pangenome size (pan_genes)`  = pan_genes
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "23 taxa common to the Kwun & Croucher HR/prophage comparison and Horsfield et al.'s Supplementary File 1, ranked by expected prophage burden.") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  scroll_box(height = "420px")
```

## 1. Pangenome size tracks prophage density

If prophage accumulation is a major contributor to pangenome expansion - as would
be expected if reduced HR allows mobile genetic elements to accumulate unchecked -
then taxa with a higher expected prophage burden should have larger pangenomes.

```{r pan-genes-vs-lambda, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_pangenome <- plot_correlation(
  full_df,
  x_var = "lambda_hat", y_var = "pan_genes",
  x_lab = "Expected number of intact Caudoviricetes prophage per genome",
  y_lab = "Pangenome size (total genes)"
)
res_pangenome$plot
```

**Figure 1.** Pangenome size (`pan_genes`, Horsfield et al. Supplementary File 1) is
strongly, positively associated with prophage density (`lambda_hat`, Kwun & Croucher).
Horizontal error bars show the 95% CI of the Poisson-fitted prophage rate;
Horsfield et al. report `pan_genes` as a point estimate with no corresponding
uncertainty, so no vertical error bars are shown.

```{r pan-genes-vs-lambda-inline, include=FALSE}
fit_pangenome <- res_pangenome$fit
```

Pangenome size and prophage density are strongly correlated
(*r* = `r round(fit_pangenome$r, 2)`, *R*^2^ = `r round(fit_pangenome$r2, 2)`,
*p* = `r format(fit_pangenome$p_value, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)`, *n* =
`r fit_pangenome$n`) - taxa with more intact prophage per genome have
systematically larger pangenomes.

### Supplementary analyses: rare genes and transformability

The same relationship holds for the count of rare accessory genes specifically
(Supplementary Figure S1), and naturally transformable taxa - which are expected to
experience more effective chromosomal curing - have significantly smaller
pangenomes on average, although this difference does not persist once prophage
density is accounted for (Supplementary Figure S2).

```{r rare-genes-vs-lambda, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_raregenes <- plot_correlation(
  full_df,
  x_var = "lambda_hat", y_var = "rare_genes",
  x_lab = "Expected number of intact Caudoviricetes prophage per genome",
  y_lab = "Number of rare accessory genes"
)
res_raregenes$plot
fit_raregenes <- res_raregenes$fit
```

**Supplementary Figure S1.** Prophage density correlates similarly strongly with
the count of rare accessory genes (*r* = `r round(fit_raregenes$r, 2)`, *p* =
`r format(fit_raregenes$p_value, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)`), consistent with
prophage themselves populating the low-frequency tail of the accessory gene
frequency distribution. As in Figure 1, only `lambda_hat` carries a reported 95%
CI, shown as horizontal error bars.

```{r transformability-vs-pangenome, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
res_transf_violin <- plot_violin_comparison(
  full_df,
  x_var = "Transformability", y_var = "pan_genes",
  x_lab = "Transformability", y_lab = "Pangenome size (total genes)"
)
res_transf_violin
```

**Supplementary Figure S2.** Naturally transformable taxa (blue) have smaller
pangenomes than non-transformable taxa (purple).

```{r transformability-joint-model}
joint_model <- lm(pan_genes ~ lambda_hat + Transformability, data = full_df)
joint_tidy  <- broom::tidy(joint_model)
transf_p    <- joint_tidy$p.value[joint_tidy$term == "TransformabilityTransformable"]
lambda_p    <- joint_tidy$p.value[joint_tidy$term == "lambda_hat"]
```

In a joint linear model of pangenome size against both prophage density and
transformability, prophage density remains a strong, significant predictor
(*p* = `r format(lambda_p, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)`) while transformability
adds no further explanatory power once prophage density is included
(*p* = `r round(transf_p, 2)`). Transformable taxa therefore have smaller
pangenomes chiefly because - consistent with the chromosomal-curing hypothesis -
they also carry fewer prophage, rather than through any additional, independent
effect of HR-mediated DNA uptake on pangenome size.

## 2. The proportion of fast genes and the Y-intercept of the core/accessory distance curve

Horsfield et al.'s model partitions the accessory genome into a small,
rapidly-exchanged ("fast") compartment and a larger, slowly-exchanged compartment;
they note that this partitioning mirrors known differences in molecular turnover
rate between mobile genetic elements and other accessory genes (citing
N'Guessan et al. 2021). If prophage density were the dominant driver of this
compartment structure, the proportion of fast genes should track `lambda_hat`
directly.

```{r propfast-vs-lambda, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_propfast_lambda <- plot_correlation(
  full_df,
  x_var = "lambda_hat", y_var = "prop_genes2_median",
  x_lab = "Expected number of intact Caudoviricetes prophage per genome",
  y_lab = "Proportion of fast genes"
)
res_propfast_lambda$plot
fit_propfast_lambda <- res_propfast_lambda$fit
```

**Supplementary Figure S3.** The proportion of fast genes is not significantly
associated with prophage density (*r* = `r round(fit_propfast_lambda$r, 2)`,
*p* = `r round(fit_propfast_lambda$p_value, 2)`).

A similar null result is seen for the raw Y-intercept of the negative-exponential
core-vs-accessory distance curve (Horsfield et al.'s instantaneous gene turnover
rate; Supplementary File 8), which is also not significantly related to prophage
density on its own:

```{r yintercept-raw-vs-lambda, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_yint_raw <- plot_correlation(
  negexp_df,
  x_var = "lambda_hat", y_var = "Y-intercept (j)_Estimate",
  x_lab = "Expected number of intact Caudoviricetes prophage per genome",
  y_lab = "Y-intercept of core/accessory distance curve"
)
res_yint_raw$plot
fit_yint_raw <- res_yint_raw$fit
```

**Supplementary Figure S4.** Raw Y-intercept vs prophage density
(*r* = `r round(fit_yint_raw$r, 2)`, *p* = `r round(fit_yint_raw$p_value, 2)`,
*n* = `r fit_yint_raw$n`).

However, the Y-intercept is a per-site rate; multiplying it by genome size converts
it into an expected number of rapidly-diverging sites genome-wide, which **does**
track prophage density closely:

```{r yintercept-scaled-vs-lambda, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_yint_scaled <- plot_correlation(
  negexp_df,
  x_var = "lambda_hat", y_var = "yint_times_genome",
  x_lab = "Expected number of intact Caudoviricetes prophage per genome",
  y_lab = "Y-intercept \u00d7 genome size"
)
res_yint_scaled$plot
fit_yint_scaled <- res_yint_scaled$fit
```

**Figure 2A (main composite figure, below).** Genome-size-scaled Y-intercept vs
prophage density (*r* = `r round(fit_yint_scaled$r, 2)`, *p* =
`r round(fit_yint_scaled$p_value, 3)`, *n* = `r fit_yint_scaled$n`).

## 3. Fast gene proportion tracks recombination probability, not prophage density

Rather than prophage density, the proportion of fast genes is far better explained
by the probability of diversification through homologous recombination:

```{r propfast-vs-hr, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_propfast_hr <- plot_correlation(
  full_df,
  x_var = "Recombination probability", y_var = "prop_genes2_median",
  x_lab = "Probability of diversification through homologous recombination",
  y_lab = "Proportion of fast genes"
)
res_propfast_hr$plot
fit_propfast_hr <- res_propfast_hr$fit
```

**Figure 2B (main composite figure, below).** Proportion of fast genes vs HR
probability (*r* = `r round(fit_propfast_hr$r, 2)`, *p* =
`r format(fit_propfast_hr$p_value, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)`, *n* =
`r fit_propfast_hr$n`).

Taxa with a higher probability of HR-mediated diversification have a
*smaller* proportion of fast genes - the opposite of what would be predicted if HR
and prophage-driven pangenome expansion were simply two aspects of the same
process. This is consistent with Horsfield et al.'s own observation that the fast
compartment is enriched for genes with mobile-genetic-element-like turnover
dynamics: where HR is frequent, chromosomal curing limits the accumulation of such
autonomously-mobile elements, shrinking the fast compartment even as `lambda_hat`
alone fails to capture this relationship directly.

## 4. Basal gene turnover tracks recombination probability, not prophage density

The same contrast holds for the basal (slow-compartment) gene turnover rate, which
is at best marginally related to prophage density on its own:

```{r baseturnover-vs-lambda, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_baseturnover_lambda <- plot_correlation(
  full_df,
  x_var = "lambda_hat", y_var = "rate_genes1_median",
  x_lab = "Expected number of intact Caudoviricetes prophage per genome",
  y_lab = "Basal gene turnover rate",
  ylim  = c(0, 0.0025)
)
res_baseturnover_lambda$plot
fit_baseturnover_lambda <- res_baseturnover_lambda$fit
```

**Supplementary Figure S5.** Basal gene turnover rate vs prophage density
(*r* = `r round(fit_baseturnover_lambda$r, 2)`, *p* =
`r round(fit_baseturnover_lambda$p_value, 2)`). The vertical axis is truncated to
emphasise the bulk of taxa; *H. influenzae* and *Neisseria* spp. have markedly
wider credible intervals that extend off the top of this view (the regression line
and statistics shown are fitted to the full, untruncated data).

```{r baseturnover-vs-hr, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
res_baseturnover_hr <- plot_correlation(
  full_df,
  x_var = "Recombination probability", y_var = "rate_genes1_median",
  x_lab = "Probability of diversification through homologous recombination",
  y_lab = "Basal gene turnover rate"
)
res_baseturnover_hr$plot
fit_baseturnover_hr <- res_baseturnover_hr$fit
```

**Figure 2C (main composite figure, below).** Basal gene turnover rate vs HR
probability (*r* = `r round(fit_baseturnover_hr$r, 2)`, *p* =
`r format(fit_baseturnover_hr$p_value, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)`, *n* =
`r fit_baseturnover_hr$n`).

Basal turnover of the slowly-exchanged gene compartment rises significantly with
HR probability. Since these are, by construction, genes that lack the
autonomous mobility of the fast compartment, this points to **transformation being
an important mechanism facilitating the exchange of accessory loci that are not
themselves autonomously mobile** - i.e. HR provides a route to exchange for genes
that would otherwise depend entirely on vertical inheritance.

## Combined summary figure

```{r combined-figure, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 4.2}
figure2 <- cowplot::plot_grid(
  res_yint_scaled$plot      + theme(legend.position = "none"),
  res_propfast_hr$plot      + theme(legend.position = "none"),
  res_baseturnover_hr$plot  + theme(legend.position = "none"),
  nrow = 1, labels = "AUTO"
)

shared_legend <- cowplot::get_plot_component(
  res_propfast_hr$plot + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal"),
  "guide-box-bottom", return_all = TRUE
)

cowplot::plot_grid(figure2, shared_legend, nrow = 2, rel_heights = c(0.88, 0.12))
```

**Figure 2.** (A) Genome-size-scaled Y-intercept vs prophage density. (B) Proportion
of fast genes vs HR probability. (C) Basal gene turnover rate vs HR probability.
Together, panels B and C show that the two components of Horsfield et al.'s
accessory-genome model are each better predicted by HR probability than by prophage
density, while panel A shows that genome-size-scaled instantaneous turnover does
track prophage density - see Discussion for how these results are reconciled.

```{r summary-table}
tibble::tribble(

  "Y-intercept \u00d7 genome size vs prophage density",    fit_yint_scaled$r,            fit_yint_scaled$r2,               fit_yint_scaled$p_value,           fit_yint_scaled$n,        "Figure 2A (main)",
  "Fast-gene proportion vs HR probability",                fit_propfast_hr$r,            fit_propfast_hr$r2,               fit_propfast_hr$p_value,           fit_propfast_hr$n,        "Figure 2B (main)",
  "Basal turnover vs prophage density",                    fit_baseturnover_lambda$r,    fit_baseturnover_lambda$r2,       fit_baseturnover_lambda$p_value,   fit_baseturnover_lambda$n,"Fig. S5",
  "Basal turnover vs HR probability",                      fit_baseturnover_hr$r,        fit_baseturnover_hr$r2,           fit_baseturnover_hr$p_value,       fit_baseturnover_hr$n,    "Figure 2C (main)"
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    r  = round(r, 3),
    R2 = round(R2, 3),
    p  = signif(p, 3)
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "Summary of all correlation statistics reported in this document (each from a single, ungrouped linear model).") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

## Discussion

### 1. Pangenome size and prophage density

Pangenome size, and the number of rare accessory genes specifically, are both
strongly positively associated with prophage density across these 23 taxa (Figure
1, Supplementary Figure S1), consistent with reduced HR allowing prophage - and the
rest of the low-frequency accessory gene pool they are embedded within - to
accumulate. Naturally transformable taxa also have significantly smaller
pangenomes on average (Supplementary Figure S2), but a joint model shows this
effect is fully accounted for by their lower prophage burden: transformability adds
no independent explanatory power once prophage density is included. This mirrors
Kwun & Croucher's own interpretation that the benefit of transformation for
chromosomal curing operates *through* its effect on prophage content, not as a
separate, direct constraint on genome size.

### 2 & 3. The accessory-genome compartment structure: fast genes track HR, not prophage

Horsfield et al. partition the accessory genome into a small, fast-exchanging
compartment and a larger, slow-exchanging one, and note that this structure mirrors
known molecular-rate differences between mobile genetic elements and other
accessory genes (citing N'Guessan et al. 2021) - i.e. there was already reason,
within Horsfield et al.'s own framework, to expect the fast compartment to be
enriched for autonomously-mobile elements such as prophage. Yet neither the
proportion of fast genes nor the (raw) instantaneous turnover rate they estimate
from the negative-exponential curve fit is significantly related to prophage
density directly (Supplementary Figures S3 and S4). Instead, both are far better
explained by HR probability: the proportion of fast genes declines significantly as
HR probability rises (Figure 2B), the inverse of the direction expected if HR and
prophage accumulation were simply two readouts of the same underlying process.

Reconciling this with the pangenome-size result in Section 1 requires distinguishing
between genome-wide pangenome *size* (which does track prophage density directly)
and the *proportion* of the accessory genome partitioned into the fast-exchanging
compartment (which does not). Genome-size-scaling resolves this: multiplying the
Y-intercept by genome size converts a per-site instantaneous turnover rate into an
expected number of rapidly-diverging sites genome-wide, and this scaled quantity
**does** track prophage density closely (Figure 2A). Taken together, these results
suggest prophage inflate the total number of rapidly-diverging genes in a genome in
absolute terms, without necessarily inflating the *proportion* of the accessory
genome behaving this way - a distinction obscured when only Horsfield et al.'s
proportional metrics are considered in isolation, and only resolved once the HR/
prophage framework is brought in as a second explanatory axis.

### 4. Basal gene turnover and HR: transformation as a route to exchange for non-mobile loci

Basal turnover of the slowly-exchanged gene compartment shows at best a marginal,
non-robust association with prophage density (Supplementary Figure S5) but rises
significantly with HR
probability (Figure 2C). Because the slow compartment is defined, by construction,
as lacking the autonomous mobility of the fast compartment, this indicates that
**transformation is an important mechanism facilitating the exchange of accessory
loci that are not themselves autonomously mobile**: in taxa where HR is frequent,
genes without their own transfer machinery can nonetheless be exchanged between
genomes via DNA uptake and recombination, raising their apparent turnover rate even
though they are not mobile genetic elements in the conventional sense.

### Overall interpretation

Across all four comparisons, a consistent pattern emerges: wherever Horsfield et
al.'s metrics are genuinely proportional or rate-based descriptions of the
accessory-genome compartment structure (proportion of fast genes, basal turnover
rate), they are better explained by HR probability than by prophage density, and in
the direction consistent with HR constraining rather than reflecting mobile
element accumulation. Wherever a metric instead captures absolute, genome-wide
quantities (pangenome size, rare gene count, genome-size-scaled turnover), prophage
density is the stronger correlate. This supports the hypothesis that the HR/
prophage conflict identified by Kwun & Croucher is one of the mechanisms underlying
the pangenome-scale variation reported by Horsfield et al., while also clarifying
that it acts on genome-wide accessory gene content and on the exchange of
non-autonomously-mobile loci, rather than uniformly reshaping the relative size of
the fast-exchanging compartment itself.

### Limitations

- The prophage estimates used throughout are restricted to geNomad-detected,
  hallmark-gene-rich *Caudoviricetes* provirus regions, deliberately excluding
  satellite phage/phage-related chromosomal islands, *Inoviridae*, and plasmids;
  the true burden of all mobile genetic elements combined is therefore larger than
  `lambda_hat` captures, and could relate differently to Horsfield et al.'s metrics.
- Sample sizes are modest (n = 23, or n = 15 for analyses requiring a Supplementary
  File 8 curve fit), and several relationships are sensitive to individual
  high-leverage taxa (e.g. *H. pylori*, *H. influenzae*).
- All comparisons are correlational and cross-sectional across taxa; they cannot
  establish the direction of causality between HR, prophage accumulation, and
  pangenome structure.
